item.title: 28 Zero-Day Findings in Under Two Days. Is Robotics Security Keeping Pace?
item.description:
This article is brought to you by VicOne.

VicOne identified an initial set of 28 zero-day findings in less than two days using AI-assisted research across software and tools supporting the Physical AI ecosystem. These include projects developed or maintained by Google, NVIDIA, and Meta, among others.

Based on initial validation, all 28 findings are classified as zero-day vulnerabilities. The count may change following vendor and vulnerability-authority review, and some findings do not yet have CVE tracking numbers.

Many of these tools help teams train, simulate, test, and operate robots. Weaknesses in them could influence the models teams build, the test results they trust, and the instructions sent to robots.

These findings create two demands for robotics teams: responding as AI helps uncover weaknesses faster, and assessing how each one could affect robot safety and operations.

What AI changes about vulnerability discovery

Vulnerability discovery involves examining code, tracing how systems communicate, and testing whether a suspected weakness can actually be exploited. AI can accelerate parts of this work, helping researchers analyze more software in less time. Attackers could use similar capabilities.

When the weakness is a zero-day — previously unknown and without an available fix — faster discovery can leave teams with little time to respond. While that exposure does not necessarily mean an attack has occurred, teams still need to determine whether they use the affected software and what an attacker could access or change.

Where the findings sit across the robot lifecycle

VicOne’s findings span three stages of the robotics lifecycle: development and training, simulation and validation, and deployment and runtime. Weaknesses at each stage could affect what a robot learns, how it is tested, and how it is controlled.

Figure 1. In this research set, 75% of findings involved development, training, simulation, or validation tools, highlighting risks that can arise before a robot is deployed.VicOne

The following scenarios show how a compromised component could influence the robot at each stage.

  • Development and training: Hidden changes can reach the finished robot
    A team downloads a pretrained model to adapt for its robot. Loading a malicious file could give an attacker access to the training system, allowing changes to training data or the model itself. A manipulated model could behave normally during routine testing but respond incorrectly to a particular object, scene, or command after deployment. The risk can enter through a tool the team trusts, before anyone attacks the robot directly.
  • Simulation and validation: A passing test could give false confidence
    Importing a compromised scene or robot model could give an attacker access to the simulation environment. With sufficient control, the attacker could alter simulated sensor readings, physical conditions, or test results. A robot could then appear to pass tests that should have exposed unsafe behavior, leading the team to approve it for real-world use on the basis of misleading evidence.
  • Deployment and runtime: Operators could lose visibility or control
    An attacker could exploit weaknesses to change files that influence motion planning or send malicious map data that crashes the operator’s monitoring display. Compromising a remote-operation computer could also put the instructions sent to the robot at risk. Depending on the system and its safeguards, these weaknesses could alter robot movement or leave operators unable to see what is happening and respond promptly.

These are potential consequences and not demonstrated outcomes for every finding. Actual effects depend on the attacker’s access, the system’s design, and whether other safeguards prevent the changes from reaching physical behavior.

In a separate demonstration, VicOne researchers provide a concrete example of a weakness affecting a protective function. The researchers exploited a vulnerability to prevent a robot’s remote-stop command from working. The case shows why teams need to test whether safeguards remain effective when the software supporting them is compromised.

Video 1. VicOne researchers demonstrate a vulnerability that prevents a robot’s remote-stop command from working. VicOne

A published patch still needs to be proven safe

AI can shorten the search for weaknesses, but a robotics team still needs to determine whether a fix is safe to deploy. Even after a software maintainer releases a patch, teams must identify affected systems, check compatibility, and verify that the update preserves intended behavior.

An earlier successful test remains useful evidence. However, a newly discovered weakness may reveal conditions that test never examined.

Three questions can help teams respond:

  • Where do we use the affected software? Include training computers, simulation environments, and deployed robots.
  • What could the weakness change? Assess whether it could affect models, test results, operator visibility, or robot behavior.
  • How do we verify protection? Confirm that the fix addresses the weakness and that the updated system still operates as intended.

When immediate updating is impractical, teams may need temporary safeguards, such as restricting access to an affected service, while a validated fix is prepared.

From discovery to safer deployment

As details from the 28 findings become available through coordinated disclosure, the next step is for robotics manufacturers is to connect each finding to its potential effect on development, deployment, and robot behavior.

That work also requires understanding how threats could affect robot behavior and how to protect systems already in operation. VicOne Radeis helps teams identify potential zero-day vulnerabilities, assess AI model and system security, and use simulation to evaluate how these risks could affect robot behavior before deployment. VicOne Rthena supports threat detection and responses within approved policies during operation.

Figure 2. Cybersecurity strengthens robot safety evidence throughout the lifecycle. VicOne helps teams test safety limits against manipulation before deployment and monitor the conditions behind safe behavior in operation.VicOne

Faster vulnerability discovery matters when teams can turn findings into action: identify what needs attention, verify that safeguards still hold, and confirm that a fix does not introduce new risks. That is how cybersecurity strengthens robot safety as systems continue to change.


For a deeper look how cybersecurity can affect robot safety, download our white paper, “Why Robot Safety Depends on Cybersecurity: Protecting the Information That Safety Decisions Rely On.”

item.title: Can Robots Bring Stroke Surgery to Remote Hospitals?
item.description:
I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach. I press a foot pedal, activating the controller in my hand, and carefully steer a thin flexible tube called a catheter up through the patient’s blood vessels. I head for what I believe to be the brain, tracking my progress on the live X-ray feed. As I imagine finding a blood clot, David Bell, the surgeon seated to my right, helpfully reminds me that every minute a stroke goes untreated, millions of brain cells suffocate, swell, and die.

The patient under the X-ray in Bell’s office is not flesh and blood, but a plastic container holding long branches of silicone tubing. The controller I hold comes from an Xbox. But the surgical robot is real. The Remedy N1 is designed for emergency operations, including thrombectomies, the standard brain operation for acute ischemic strokes caused by blood clots. Ischemia, a restriction of blood flow, is the most common cause of stroke.

“We want it to feel a bit like a video game—a bit easy,” Bell says. “But we don’t want to dehumanize it as if there’s just another ‘game over.’ ” Bell, a clinician and former cardiac-surgery trainee from Australia, cofounded Remedy Robotics, based in San Francisco. With a team of engineers, he developed this robotic catheter and its related software to help ischemic stroke patients in remote and rural places, who lose crucial hours while being transferred away from hospitals incapable of providing care. According to 2025 data, at least 5 million people around the world suffer ischemic strokes every year. In the United States, stroke is the fourth leading cause of death.

When Remedy Robotics cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell initially met, they matched each other’s energy right away.Christie Hemm Klok

The screen shows my catheter at a fork in the narrowing road, and I decide to take a sharp right; I think I can make it. This device feels easier to drive than a typical robotic instrument that I controlled on a hospital tour the summer prior. I say to Bell that here my movements are smoother, more precise—exactly the talking point you’d expect to hear from a surgical robotics company. Never mind that, Bell corrects me: “Smoothness and precision are not clinical outcomes. Neither is a surgeon’s ergonomics.”

For Bell, the outcome that matters is whether the robot can get stroke treatment to patients who otherwise wouldn’t receive it in time. Today, only about 1 in 10 patients eligible for thrombectomy receive one. That’s where the long-unrealized promise of telesurgery is meeting an urgent problem: providing access to thrombectomies before life-threatening damage takes hold.

But can putting a robot in one hospital and a surgeon somewhere else actually close that gap? Remedy has already taken a first step, remotely testing its system on a small group of patients. “The remote stroke need is well known,” says Jake Sganga, who cofounded Remedy with Bell and leads the technology side. “It’s just a hard problem to take on.” Making telesurgery a practical part of stroke care will require more than a capable robot: It will depend on communications infrastructure, hospital resources and workflows, and ultimately, evidence that patients actually benefit.

Why Telesurgery Starts With Stroke

As recently as the early ’90s, physicians who treated stroke struggled with “therapeutic nihilism.” A 1991 editorial by two lamenting neurologists expressed hope that a successful drug therapy for stroke would emerge that would “reverse the trend of nihilism.” Five years later, clot-busting drugs revolutionized stroke treatment, followed about a decade later by mechanical thrombectomy, in which a blood clot is physically removed from an artery.

In a standard thrombectomy a surgeon snakes a flexible wire through a small opening in the patient’s groin. This guide wire sets the route for a fine hollow tube around it, the catheter, to travel through the blood vessels to the brain, where instruments remove the clot. Suddenly a stroke was no longer a sentence of profound disability or death but a treatable event.

Yet decades later, thrombectomies remain inherently blind expeditions. The surgeon stands beside the patient, physically pushing these lines up, inch by inch. The only view comes from a live X-ray, which can’t see soft tissues like blood vessels. The surgeon shoots brief puffs of contrast dye through the catheter to illuminate the path ahead. A nimble operator can avoid scraping or piercing artery walls while bending the guide wire’s rounded tip around corners. But even these left or right turns are not intuitive. The guide wire can twist inside the body, and because the surgeon sees only a flat silhouette, steering it left may actually rotate the guidewire to the right.

The N1 robot feeds the catheter along a rail lined with seven modules, using a thin wire that allows precise control through a patient’s vascular system, even from kilometers away. Christie Hemm Klok

If all goes as planned, the doctor reaches the brain and pushes instruments through the catheter to dislodge the clot, then carefully pulls everything back out. Bell remembers how thrombectomies felt when he performed them. “I’m one and a half meters away from my catheter tip. I’m not in control of it. I can’t see where the blood vessels are. I thought, what is the ideal way to do these procedures? It’s certainly not what I’m doing now.”

Sganga and Bell want their robots to do two things: see what surgeons can’t see and be where surgeons can’t be. When I visited Remedy’s office in January, the team showed me their robotic arm and instruments that snap onto it. Motorized cartridges live on the robotic arm, one containing several actuators that use small gears to grip the threadlike instruments to move them in and out of a body. The instruments include a stent, an expandable wire-mesh tube used to pierce, grab, and yank a clot back out. It’s all typical stroke operation equipment—except for the catheter.

Remedy’s catheter is steerable, so it doesn’t need a guide wire to pave its path. Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream. As I maneuver the catheter with the Xbox controller, Bell and Sganga tell me they made wayfinding a priority. Sganga toggles on a CT scan to overlay on the X-ray feed. Suddenly I see the bright three-dimensional routes of blood vessels along a path that had been invisible on X-ray.

I noticed a pattern of small markings on the catheter. Sganga tells me they’re not for the surgeon, but for a computer-vision algorithm that tracks the catheter’s rotation inside the body. If an operator wants to steer right, Remedy’s software automatically translates that intention into the correct action. Instead of squinting at a 2D silhouette on an X-ray and mentally compensating for every twist in the catheter, the surgeon simply toggles to the right on the X-ray image, the Remedy system adjusts, and the catheter moves in the correct direction.

This system grew out of ideas that Bell and Sganga were pursuing when they met at Stanford in 2019. Already a physician, Bell was completing an MBA and enrolled in a robotics class in hopes of meeting an engineer who might share his interest in creating a medical robot. The professor connected him to Sganga, a bioengineering doctoral student who was developing pathfinding algorithms for an FDA-approved robotic bronchoscope to navigate the lungs.

Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream.

Sganga’s engineering work had exposed him to surgical robotics companies that failed because they hadn’t chosen a valuable enough problem to solve. He sought a medical problem where a robot could prove its worth well before human trials, and stroke stood out. “It’s an already verified clinical need,” Sganga says, “Time.” When he and Bell met for coffee, they matched each other’s energy right away: “It was like ‘Hey how you doing?’ and then we were looking at medical images of blood vessels together off of his phone,” Sganga says.

About a year after they both left Stanford, Bell and Sganga rented a two-car garage in Southern California and X-ray-proofed it with lead lining. “We called it the bunker because it had exposed lead on all sides, including the ceiling,” Sganga says. “It was just big enough to fit a bed and this rickety old C-arm [X-ray].” There they test-drove a prototype of their steerable catheter through silicone arteries—first controlling the robot on-site from another room, and then from a laptop hundreds of kilometers away. “We were trying to get an initial sign of life,” Sganga says. “And it was that moment that we realized that this could work.”

Telesurgery’s Second Act

Dreams of remote surgery predate modern stroke care. In the 1980s and 1990s, the companies Computer Motion and Intuitive developed bedside robots to assist surgeons. Then, in 2001, French surgeon Jacques Marescaux and Canadian surgeon Michel Gagner removed a patient’s gallbladder from more than 6,000 km away. In New York City, Marescaux used a computer connected via high-speed fiber optics to control a Computer Motion robot in Strasbourg, France. The milestone, known as the Lindbergh Operation, was completed safely with no complications.

But telesurgery did not take off after Lindbergh. Instead, companies invested in robots operated by surgeons in the same room. Computer Motion and Intuitive merged in 2003, more companies sprang up, and robotic surgery steadily entered the mainstream. Today thousands of surgical robots operate in hospitals around the country, assisting in roughly 22 percent of surgeries. In 2023 alone, more than 2 million surgeries were performed with da Vinci, Intuitive’s flagship platform.

Remedy mechanical engineer Chris Hapstack [left] and software engineer Campbell Crowley adjust the N1 robot. Christie Hemm Klok

In the summer of 2025, telesurgery appeared to regain momentum when surgeons near Orlando, Fla., removed the prostate from a man 11,000 km away in Luanda, Angola. Around the same time, Intuitive demonstrated what it called “telecollaboration,” in which two surgeons on different continents operated together on a tissue model. Meanwhile, India-based SS Innovations has been testing cardiac telesurgery; in Panama, the Texas-based medical robotics company XCath has tested a steerable guide wire for thrombectomies. These companies are building on advances in computer vision and machine learning, yet remote robotics is hardly a sure bet.

“The first procedures are going to be those procedures where time is critical,” says Brad Nelson, who develops surgical robots at ETH Zurich and is not affiliated with Remedy. Last year, Nelson coauthored a report in Science Robotics arguing that telesurgery’s future success hinges on finding emergency operations where patients can’t always reach specialists in time, including stroke, heart attack, and fetal operations.

Surgeries that occur within blood vessels seem an attractive proving ground for teleoperation in emergencies. “If you have a hiccup, the nice thing about vascular procedures is nothing bad can happen other than the thing stops moving,” Nelson says. There’s neither a large open cavity to tend to, nor the urgent choreography one might need in organ transplants. If the surgeon loses connection to the robot while the catheter is inside a blood vessel, the operation can pause in place without damage.

Nelson’s lab is also working on a stroke solution. He has partnered with the Mayo Clinic in Arizona to build microscopic robots—the size of a coffee grain—steered with magnets to dissolve a clot.

When Surgery Depends on the Network

After preliminary success in the garage, Sganga and Bell turned their focus to the environment where the Remedy N1 would live. Doctors and nurses advised them to improve the live audio-video feed, as any surgery is a coordinated team effort requiring constant communication. They were told to improve setup time, maintenance, cleaning, and began a series of conversations about secure communication and cybersecurity.

In 2021, CEO David Bell naps next to Remedy’s first X-ray machine in a lead-lined garage in Venice, Calif. Remedy Robotics

Absent a cyberattack, the elephant in the room for any telesurgery hopeful is latency. Experts speak about latency, or lag, in terms of how many thousandths of a second it takes for a small packet of data to reach a destination then ping back to its original source. In a major city with strong 5G or fiber-optic internet, latency might measure in the tens of milliseconds. In rural areas, even in the United States, lag can drag above 100.

Noticeable lag may not be a dealbreaker. When researchers in Japan analyzed five years of surgical simulations and demonstrations, they reported surgeons adapting to the connection speed. They paused. They moved more slowly. Remedy has noticed similar behavior in test runs. “We’ve actually found that operators are quite resilient to latency,” Sganga says.

Still, Remedy targets a round-trip latency of no more than 150 milliseconds, below the average human reaction time of 200 milliseconds. Whenever latency sneaks above that threshold, the system pauses all surgical action. Bell and Sganga say they’ve tailored their system to work with the slower internet speeds common in rural areas that would benefit from better access to stroke care, claiming they recently operated their system from across the Pacific using a mobile hotspot.

But sorting out the engineering details raises more questions about how telesurgery might change surgical practice. Bell told me he worries about what a telesurgical future could bring. What if surgeons’ skills erode? What if trainees become dependent on specific platforms? What if two patients need care from the same remote surgeon at the same time? “Is the person suffering a stroke in America necessarily more important than the person suffering a stroke in India? No,” Bell says. “So how do you figure that out? That’s something I think about a lot.”

Where Telesurgery Could Work Best

During a stroke, a blockage in the brain triggers symptoms within seconds or minutes. The following hour is the so-called golden period for saving the brain before the risk of permanent damage grows. “Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die,” says neurologist Archit Bhatt of Providence Medical Group in Portland, Oregon. “You really need to act fast.” Yet decades after the advent of thrombectomies, one in five Americans lives more than an hour from a hospital that offers the procedure.

Medium and small hospitals often lack the 24-hour surgical team, experience, or equipment for thrombectomies, so they must transfer stroke patients to large hospitals. As a result, standard stroke care is concentrated in urban areas. For example, Alaska’s only two thrombectomy centers serving the 739,000 people who live or work in the state are both in Anchorage, leaving more than half of residents out of range.

But the places most in need of telesurgery may also be the hardest places to deploy it. For starters, they may not have the high-quality network connections that remote surgery requires. Last June, experts from five major robotic corporations coauthored a list of technical standards for what they called “surgical-grade networks.” Mike Teodorescu, an information systems researcher with the University of Washington, says experts usually consider 100 milliseconds a safe threshold, but his team recently reported that many rural communities—and even most countries—struggle to meet it.

Neuroradiologist Hal Rice of the Australian Stroke Alliance remotely operates Remedy’s N1 System.Remedy Robotics

And connectivity is only part of the problem. The smallest and most remote hospitals may lack other support needed for thrombectomy, including neurologists, catheterization teams, CT scanners, and specialized intensive care units. “It’s an infrastructure problem,” Teodorescu says.

Medium-size regional hospitals may be a better target. Although they rarely offer thrombectomies, many already have the right support, experience, and patient volume. “There is a window for a thrombectomy center in a reasonably sized town where there is a stable economy,” says neurologist Bhatt.

“Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die.”–neurologist Archit Bhatt

Telesurgery could do more than bring a distant specialist into the operating room. Jasdeep Bahra, an emergency medicine physician and lecturer in Kilifi, Kenya, worries that telerobotics could concentrate expertise in cities—widening the skill gap between rich cities and poor towns. The thrombectomy access problem is real, Bahra says, but lower income communities might benefit more if a system like Remedy’s could both treat patients and help train clinicians on-site. Sganga says Bahra’s idea fits Remedy’s mission.

“Digital operating rooms where you have surgeons that are over your shoulder as a mentor,” Bahra says. “If that’s what we’re talking about in telesurgery, that is the future for me.”

Measures of Success

If smoothness and precision aren’t clinical outcomes, as Bell told me, what would count as success? One target is safety. In more than 1 percent of thrombectomy operations, surgeons unintentionally slice open a blood vessel, a feared and sometimes fatal occurrence that Bell believes robots can prevent.

In September 2025, Bell flew to Toronto for Remedy’s first test in human patients. Ten patients had consented to nonemergency procedures with Remedy’s robot. A neurosurgeon with a laptop would operate on six patients in an adjoining room; two elsewhere in the hospital; and two at an entirely different hospital across town. The Remedy team had experimented for years on silicone models, like the one I test-drove. Tests on lab animals suggested that, compared with a human, their robot collided less often with blood vessels and finished procedures faster.

Neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira pilots the N1 system in 2024 for its first in-person robotic procedure, in Toronto. Remedy Robotics

In the run-up to the Toronto procedures, the team measured internet latencies meticulously. Now they could only hope that their results would translate to human patients. “You’re never sure of how that leap is going to look, and it’s actually really hard to test,” Bell says. The night before the first operation, Bell barely slept.

The procedures—recording images called angiograms from within patients’ blood vessels—were a success, and were completed nearly twice as quickly as the current standard. “I cannot explain the relief,” Bell says. Remedy considers speed one measure of success because it can allow doctors to treat more people.

In 2025, neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira and his team at Unity Health Toronto perform the first fully remote robotic neurointerventional procedures. Remedy Robotics

A few months after my visit, Remedy announced US $62 million in new funding to support upcoming clinical trials. A portion of that investment came from the University of California system, which will host the clinical studies within a year, according to Bell. Remedy’s first trials will be on-site elective procedures, such as treating unruptured aneurysms, before expanding to remote surgeries in Australia or within the University of California system, near the end of 2027.

Sganga emphasizes that the on-site trials are not just a stepping stone. He’s come to believe that Remedy’s success depends on improving operations even when the surgeon is in the room. “The remote solution—it’s very flashy, it’s very obvious what that patient need is—but in order to get there, we believe you have to solve a meaningful problem on-premise,” he says. “Otherwise, doctors simply won’t use the system, and if they don’t use the system, they’re not going to gain the expertise required to operate remotely.”

The steerable catheter and computer-vision algorithm are two features he claims will improve thrombectomies, remote or not. And as trials ramp up, Sganga says they will look at factors beyond safety and surgical speed. “How quickly are doctors picking up on this new technique? How smoothly are the bedside interactions going? How quickly are folks able to set up the draping and interact with the tools?” he says. Bell has wondered whether to add a photo or video of the patient’s face to the surgeon’s display to preserve the emotional stakes of surgery.

These ambitions draw Bell and Sganga’s 25-person company into uncharted waters. Beyond one-time demonstrations, no robotics company has earned full regulatory approval for telesurgery, and no patient has been operated on remotely in the United States. Remedy hopes to change that. Decades after stroke research conquered the “therapeutic nihilism” that once defined the field, Remedy hopes telesurgery can bring thrombectomy to everyone who needs it, no matter where they might be.

item.title: Critical Java Vulnerability Requires Immediate Patching
item.description:
Purpose

CISA strongly urges organizations to immediately patch the recently disclosed Oracle Java vulnerability CVE-2026-114938. This critical memory-corruption vulnerability, known as “Java4Shell,” affects the Base64 decoder of the x86-64 HotSpot Java Virtual Machine (JVM), which is part of the Java Development Kit (JDK). Specially crafted Base64 input could crash the JVM and allow for unauthenticated remote code execution.

Actions to take

CISA urges organizations to take the following actions:

  • Identify affected Java installations. Review your software inventory for JDKs and Java runtimes, including those bundled with third-party applications or included in container images and appliances. Note: JDKs and Java runtimes may not appear as separate entries in software inventories.
  • Apply relevant Java and vendor patches as soon as they are available, prioritizing internet-facing systems.
    • If immediate patching is not feasible, implement temporary compensating controls, such as restricting and validating Base64 input at the application boundary, enforcing input-size limits, and limiting unauthenticated access.
  • Review Oracle’s security advisory for guidance on patching and affected products and versions.
  •  Monitor for indicators of suspicious activity, including rogue runtimes, unexpected JVM crashes, and suspicious Java processes.

item.title: oPt: Gaza's Education Crisis: A System-Wide Collapse Threatening an Entire Generation
item.description:
Country: occupied Palestinian territory
Source: American Near East Refugee Aid

Please refer to the attached file.

AN ENTIRE GENERATION OUT OF SCHOOL

The war that began on October 7, 2023 did not just interrupt schooling in Gaza, it dismantled the education system that more than 750,000 learners, from preschool through university, once relied on.1 Nearly all schools have been damaged or destroyed, and for over two years, students of all ages have had little to no access to formal learning.

A child who was seven when this began is now nine or ten, and has spent a third of the life that they can remember waiting for school to resume.

This report is based on Anera's Gaza Education Sector Needs Assessment, which draws on interviews and focus group discussions with teachers, parents, students, education officials and community members across Gaza, alongside secondary data from UNRWA, UNICEF, the Education Cluster, the Palestine Central Bureau of Statistics and other humanitarian and education partners.

What emerges is a story of systemic collapse in education, one that has stripped away not just classrooms, but the routines, relationships and sense of future that schooling once provided. The war's psychological toll is equally profound. Children have endured repeated familial displacement, loss and violence, while teachers are coping with their own trauma even as they try to support students.

Yet, despite overwhelming challenges, Gaza's communities continue to demonstrate remarkable tenacity. Parents, volunteers and educators have created informal classrooms and learning activities wherever possible, underscoring the determination to keep young people learning and the urgent need for sustained international support. Children cannot recover academically without first having stability, routine and protection. Restoring education in Gaza should therefore begin with three essentials: safe places to learn, teachers who are supported and able to teach, and basic classroom resources.

This report tells the story of what has been lost and lays out what must happen next.

item.title: Afghanistan: Humanitarian Update, October 2026
item.description:
Country: Afghanistan
Source: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs

Please refer to the attached file.

Funding shortfalls threaten winter response in Afghanistan

As temperatures begin to fall across Afghanistan, humanitarian partners are ramping up winter preparedness amid significant funding constraints. Aid organizations are pre-positioning supplies to enable them to deliver assistance before access to remote communities becomes more challenging. With needs expected to remain high, the humanitarian response enters the winter season facing a substantial funding gap, raising concerns about being able to reach all those in need and forcing difficult choices about how the limited resources are prioritized.

The 2026 Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan requires US$1.71 billion to provide life-saving assistance and protection across Afghanistan. However, as of October, only $550 million has been received through the Plan, meaning 68 per cent of funding requirements remain unmet. This shortfall threatens efforts to support vulnerable communities during one of the most challenging seasons of the year.

Winter often brings heightened humanitarian risks across Afghanistan. In many provinces, heavy snowfall and freezing temperatures can isolate communities, disrupt transportation routes and limit access to markets, health facilities and other essential services. For households already struggling with poverty, food insecurity, climate-related shocks and limited livelihood opportunities, the cold season brings additional pressure as families seek to secure food, heating fuel, warm clothing and adequate shelter.

As winter approaches, many vulnerable families are expected to face increasing pressure as food prices, heating costs and other seasonal expenses rise while livelihood opportunities decline. Yet several critical sectors remain significantly underfunded.

Food Security and Agriculture, the largest sector in the humanitarian response, has received only 18.2 per cent of its funding requirements despite continued concerns over food insecurity across the country. As winter conditions reduce income-generating opportunities and increase household expenditure on food, fuel and other essentials, many families are likely to face greater difficulties in meeting their basic needs.

Emergency Shelter and Non-Food Items cluster, which provides vulnerable households with shelter support, essential household items and winter assistance, has received only 15.1 per cent of the funding required. Water, Sanitation and Hygiene programmes are similarly underfunded, with just 16.6 per cent of requirements met, while Nutrition activities have received 16.3 per cent. Health is funded at 45.4 per cent, leaving significant gaps in essential services, particularly as winter conditions increase the risk of respiratory infections and other seasonal illnesses.

Together, these funding shortfalls risk limiting access to food, shelter, health care, safe water and nutrition support during one of the most challenging periods of the year, potentially leaving vulnerable households with fewer options to cope.

item.title: In South Sudan, New Lifelines for Mothers and Babies
item.description:
Country: South Sudan
Source: Direct Relief

In a region where pregnant women still face dangerous journeys to give birth, emergency transportation and medical supplies are helping transform maternal care.

On September 21, a pregnant woman collapsed in a remote South Sudanese town, where reaching a hospital can mean hours of travel along roads that become nearly impassable in the rainy season.

But for the first time, help came on three wheels.

One of four newly launched motorcycle ambulances rushed the woman to Mother Teresa Hospital, marking a lifesaving first-day test of an emergency transport system designed to reach mothers in some of the country’s most isolated communities, including displacement camps.

South Sudan has the world’s highest estimated neonatal mortality rate, with roughly one in 25 babies dying within their first 28 days of life, according to United Nations Inter-agency Group for Child Mortality Estimation data published last year. South Sudan also has one of the world’s highest maternal mortality rates, with an estimated 692 deaths per 100,000 live births in 2023.

Against that backdrop, local health workers report a striking development.

“It has given us the good news up to now. We have no neonatal deaths and no deaths of the mother,” said Joseph Makuach, health coordinator for Transformation of the World in Christ, or TWIC, a local organization, which shares its acronym with the South Sudanese county of Twic, that coordinates medical services.

Working alongside a network of community clinics and Mother Teresa Hospital, the ambulance, which was funded by Direct Relief partner MAMA Project, transports women in labor and patients experiencing obstetric emergencies to facilities equipped to provide care. Recent shipments of midwife kits from Direct Relief have added essential supplies needed for safer deliveries.

Reaching Mothers Before It’s Too Late

TWIC, the nonprofit, supports six primary health care clinics serving rural communities and internally displaced people. The clinics are located in Ayak Makot, Biemnhom, Bombil, Akotong, Madou, and Gogrial West.

The new fleet of motorcycle ambulances, built in Uganda, helps connect these communities with Mother Teresa Hospital and other local healthcare facilities operated by international NGOs. The vehicles have proved unexpectedly effective in difficult terrain. Unlike heavier ambulances, the motorcycles can navigate narrow, damaged roads and can be pushed free when they become stuck in mud.

When a woman needs emergency transport, community members contact TWIC staff, who coordinate with drivers and the receiving hospital. The vehicles have drivers and fuel available to respond.

The Supplies Behind Safer Deliveries

Transportation, however, is only part of the challenge.

Mother Teresa Hospital, the principal referral hospital in Twic County, has long struggled with shortages of essential medical supplies and adequately compensated health workers.

Direct Relief recently provided 15 midwife kits through TWIC’s partner network, with distributions to Mother Teresa Hospital, Lighthouse Hospital in Aweil, and nursing and midwifery partners associated with Juba Teaching Hospital.

The donated supplies include sterile gauze, gloves, umbilical cord clamps, disinfectants, and medicines such as magnesium sulfate and misoprostol, used in managing complications of pregnancy and childbirth. Together, the materials help health workers maintain hygienic conditions and respond to emergencies.

Dr. Luka Matik, director of Mother Teresa Hospital, said the supplies have improved conditions for mothers and newborns during both vaginal and cesarean deliveries.

“Safety and hygiene, they ensure safety for the mothers and babies,” Matik said, explaining that clean delivery practices reduce the risk of infections.

Matik said deliveries at the hospital have increased since the kits arrived, an indication, he believes, that women are gaining confidence in the care available.

“If a mother comes and delivers and sees she’s well taken care of, she will go ahead and spread the word,” he said.

In October, the hospital performed 20 cesarean sections, including procedures for women referred from surrounding health facilities.

The impact of the donated supplies extends to Aweil, in neighboring Northern Bahr el Ghazal state. At Lighthouse Hospital and its outreach centers, health workers recorded 180 deliveries resulting in 182 newborns in October, according to a report submitted to Direct Relief. The facilities also provided antenatal care to 480 clients and referred five women to Aweil Civil Hospital for cesarean sections. No maternal deaths were recorded during the month.

For Teresa Paul, a midwife at Lighthouse Hospital, the difference is apparent when women arrive in labor, particularly at night.

“Before the kits arrived, we often struggled with shortages of gloves, plastic sheets, cord clamps and chlorhexidine,” she said in a statement included in the hospital’s report. “When a mother came into labor at night, and supplies were not available, it was heartbreaking.”

“Now we can reassure mothers that essential delivery supplies are ready.”

For some patients, the benefits are also financial. Mary Abuk Garang, a 32-year-old mother who received care at Lighthouse Hospital, said she arrived without the supplies needed for childbirth.

“I came with nothing, but I received what I needed for my delivery,” she said in a testimonial provided by the hospital.

Dr. Repent Khamis George, principal of the Juba College of Nursing and Midwives, said midwife kits were distributed to three primary health care centers around Juba, the nation’s capital, where staff welcomed supplies that are often difficult to obtain.

Progress Amid Persistent Shortages

Despite the reported improvements, formidable challenges remain.

Matik said Mother Teresa Hospital needs additional surgical nurses, disinfectants, cleaning materials, intravenous fluids, catheters, and basic linens. Some health workers have gone months without government-funded incentive payments, placing additional pressure on colleagues supported by TWIC.

Even as these personnel challenges and other stark issues remain, Makuach, TWIC’s health coordinator, assessed recent developments in lives saved.

“Our situation is not like before,” he said.

Since 2025, Direct Relief has provided $3.2 million in medical aid to support the health work of Transformation of the World in Christ in South Sudan.

item.title: World: MSF calls for stronger AMR response to protect people affected by conflict
item.description:
Country: World
Source: Médecins Sans Frontières

Rome, 18 Nov 26 - As the world marks World Antimicrobial Resistance (AMR) Awareness Week, MSF called on governments and funders to recognize the enormous toll that antimicrobial resistance is taking in conflict-affected and humanitarian contexts and act urgently by better equipping communities to prevent, detect, and respond to drug-resistant infections - before, during, and after times of acute crisis. Over two billion people are estimated to live in conflict-affected settings, and, in 2025, forced displacement affected an unprecedented 122 million people.

In specific, at the Fourth Plenary Assembly of the AMR Multi-Stakeholder Partnership Platform held in Rome, Italy this week, MSF asked governments and funders to:

• Invest before crises to fund national AMR plans that strengthen infection prevention and control (IPC), water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), stewardship and laboratories

• Plan for crises along with affected communities to build AMR into emergency preparedness and adapt national AMR plans in protracted crises, implementing context-specific interventions

• Protect health care to uphold international humanitarian law

• Count everyone to include conflict settings in surveillance and research, and ensure equitable access to antimicrobials and diagnostics

“For the people we treat, antimicrobial resistance is not a 2050 projection. It is a newborn with sepsis, or a person with a war wound, whose infection no longer responds to the antibiotics we have,” said Dr Cecilia Ferreyra, infectious diseases specialist and Deputy to the International Medical Secretary of MSF. “The global fight against antimicrobial resistance will fail if it leaves behind people who are living through conflict and displacement. We are asking governments and donors for dedicated funding and adapted national AMR plans that include people vulnerable to crises from the start. The commitments made here and in the Ministerial Conference in Abuja next month will help decide whether these patients still have medical tools that work.”

The risks and consequences of AMR are especially acute in settings affected by conflict and humanitarian crises, where inadequate WASH measures, poor infection prevention and control, and limited access to microbiology, diagnostic capacity, and appropriate antimicrobials contribute to emergence and spread of drug-resistant infections. Destruction of healthcare facilities and infrastructure for water and sanitation, shortages of healthcare workers, disrupted supply chains, and overcrowded living conditions further compound the AMR crisis. ​

MSF addresses AMR in more than 20 countries through over 50 projects, focusing on infection prevention and control, antibiotic stewardship, microbiology-based diagnostics, and surveillance. Our teams see the diversity of ways in which crises subject people to risk for and from AMR. From treating patients with severe wounds and drug-resistant infections to caring for malnourished children and newborns with sepsis, and people living with HIV who develop opportunistic infections, MSF works to strengthen healthcare workers’ capacity to counter AMR through provision of quality, people-centered care.

“Antimicrobial resistance is increasingly becoming a consequence of conflict, displacement and fragile health systems,” said Dr Rupa Kanapathipillai, Antimicrobial Stewardship Lead, MSF Operational Centre Paris. “In Gaza, facilities designed for 250–300 patients a day received as many as 700, with wound care provided from shared trolleys. In South Sudan, Ethiopia and Nigeria, where displacement, flooding and outbreaks hit already stretched clinics, premature babies with sepsis and severely malnourished children are being treated where our antibiograms show high resistance, even in remote areas. Resistance follows displacement and weak health systems, not just the front line.”

Global initiatives, including the updated Global Action Plan on AMR (adopted in May 2026), the planned launch of the Independent Panel for Evidence for Action against AMR, at the 5th Global High-Level Ministerial Conference on AMR in Abuja, Nigeria (6–8 December 2026), offer important opportunities to accelerate action. These initiatives are particularly crucial in light of recent shocks to global health and humanitarian financing that are taking us backwards rather than ahead. ​

“At the upcoming Ministerial Conference in Nigeria, governments must make concrete commitments and ensure that the Independent Panel on Evidence for Action against AMR will close critical evidence gaps in conflict-affected and humanitarian settings and translating evidence into action,” said Pauline Londeix, Advocacy Advisor, MSF Access. “Meaningful representation of humanitarian actors, affected communities and low-income countries is also essential to guarantee the Panel’s work responds to the needs of people most at risk.”

item.title: Drone strikes in Sudan leave children with nowhere to escape as conflict worsens
item.description:
Country: Sudan
Source: World Vision
  • More than 800 civilians, including children, have been killed with nearly 100,000 in Blue Nile displaced
  • This month 25 strikes have been recorded in 11 states, with hospitals, power stations, markets and homes all being targeted
  • World Vision calls on all sides to stop killing children and let essential aid flow

Drone strikes are killing hundreds of people in Sudan every month, leaving children and families facing hunger, a lack of clean water, and increased security risks as the number of drone strikes continues to escalate, says World Vision, which is calling on all sides to stop targeting civilians.

At least 880 civilians have been killed between January and May 2026, accounting for approximately 80 per cent of all civilian deaths. Civilians are being killed in markets, hospitals, displacement camps, and transport hubs.

TJ Grant, National Director, World Vision New Zealand, says, "Children and civilians are not collateral damage. Even if they aren’t targeted directly, they are the ones that suffer the consequences when essential services are targeted."

"Without power clean water cannot be pumped, hospitals can’t function, and health centres can’t keep medicines and vaccines safe. Parents risk their lives every time they go to the market to buy food. Aid agencies are also facing tough choices, often forced to cancel aid trips due to drone activity, leaving thousands without the vital support they desperately need."

Last month alone, more than 300 people in Sudan were killed, most of them civilians.

At least 25 strikes have been recorded across 11 states so far this month, including areas far from active frontlines. In Damazin, the Blue Nile State capital, drone strikes hit the Rosieres Dam Transmission Station and the city’s power plant, cutting electricity.

The situation is worsening, according to the latest figures from the Sudan INGO Forum, of which World Vision is a member. Attacks on infrastructure are impacting power supplies, health care provisions, and people’s ability to buy food and fuel. In one day alone, drones struck six power stations, disrupting electricity across south-east Sudan.

Simon Mane, National Director for World Vision Sudan, says: "This must stop. Children and civilians have already fled fighting. Now the drones are following them, leaving them with no place to run."

Mass casualty incidents are also increasing. A 26 October attack on a market in Nyala, South Darfur, killed or injured more than 150 people, while a drone strike near Amiet Market and Todach in the Abyei area on 19 October left dozens more civilians dead or injured.

Mane says, "Drones are targeting the power, fuel, and water supplies people depend on to survive. When a power station is hit, the consequences reach far beyond the site itself, affecting a child on oxygen in hospital, a patient needing dialysis, and families are left without access to clean water."

Security conditions in Blue Nile continue to deteriorate, with nearly 100,000 people displaced and growing fears of hunger as El Niño threatens the critical harvest season.

World Vision Sudan staff are providing life-saving assistance to hundreds of thousands of children and families on both sides of the conflict. However, movement restrictions, fuel shortages, and rising costs are making it difficult to reach those in need.

World Vision calls for all sides to:

  • Stop targeting civilians and essential infrastructure (power, fuel and water systems)
  • Protect displacement sites from fighting
  • Permit humanitarian access and support for displaced and host communities affected by ongoing violence
  • Allow civilians to access farms, grazing lands, and agricultural and market infrastructure during this critical harvest period to prevent widespread hunger

item.title: World: Start Fund Monthly Risk Bulletin (Issued: November 2026)
item.description:
Countries: World, Burundi, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Ethiopia, Lebanon, Mozambique, occupied Palestinian territory, South Sudan, Syrian Arab Republic, Uganda, United Republic of Tanzania, Zambia, Zimbabwe
Source: Start Network

Please refer to the attached file.

The Start Fund monthly Risk Bulletin reports on new, emerging or deteriorating situations. It is collated by the Start Fund Anticipation team using a range of online sources. Key risks are shared and collated each month. Ongoing events that are considered to be unchanged are not featured, and risks that are beyond the scope and scale of the Start Fund are also not featured.

Anticipated hazards considered high priority in this month’s edition include:

  • Flooding in Ethiopia, South Sudan, Uganda, northeastern DRC, Burundi and Tanzania- Disease Outbreaks in Zambia, Zimbabwe, and Mozambique
  • Start Network members interested in raising an anticipation alert for any of the risks highlighted in the bulletin can email startfund@startnetwork.org.
